articleSummary: Angiostrongylus cantonensis infection from garden slugs and snails poses a risk to humans and pets in home gardens. The disease, angiostrongyliasis or eosinophilic meningitis, results when people ingest raw or undercooked molluscs or produce contaminated with mollusk larvae. After ingestion, larvae migrate to the brain and central nervous system causing severe headache, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting, and potentially neurological deficits. Dogs are especially at risk, with Angiostrongylus infections causing respiratory issues, weight loss, and coagulation problems, which can be fatal if untreated. Prevention emphasizes thorough washing of garden produce (lettuce, kale) and soaking in sodium hypochlorite solution before consumption. For mollusk control, avoid toxic poisons; use barriers like crushed eggshells or coffee grounds. Supervise pets after rain; prevent access to standing water and keep pet bowls clean and protected.

articleSummary: Jakarta, Indonesia—The World Health Organization issued new tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis guidelines, endorsing near-point-of-care molecular testing to diagnose TB for the first time, alongside easily collected swab (saliva) testing to broaden access. A low-cost sputum-collection strategy is also recommended to improve testing efficiency for initial TB detection and rifampicin resistance. The guidelines aim to close persistent diagnostic gaps that leave millions with delayed or missed TB diagnoses, due to reliance on sputum samples not producible by all patients, limited lab availability, and high costs. The recommendations specify near-point-of-care testing for TB without rifampicin resistance at peripheral health facilities and communities; swab specimens used with NPOC; sputum-based testing using LC-NAAT to detect rifampicin resistance where resources permit. WHO urges rapid adoption to enable earlier TB diagnosis, per Dr. Tereza Kasaeva.

articleSummary: Rabies vaccination is strongly recommended for travelers to avoid a disease with little treatment once symptoms appear. While rabies is rare in Germany and Europe, India and other countries in South and Southeast Asia, and Africa pose risk for long-term travelers, adventure tourists, and people with frequent animal contact. Children are particularly at risk due to higher bite rates from dogs. Transmission chiefly occurs through dog bites or scratches, or dog saliva. Germany uses two inactivated-virus vaccines; after three doses at 1–3 week intervals, individuals are protected. If exposed after incomplete immunization, a booster is advised, ideally the same day, with a possible second booster after three days. In non-immunized exposures in endemic areas, active vaccination plus passive immunoglobulins may be required, though availability can be limited. articleSummary: Nature Health Global (NHG) released in August 2025 a study in mBio—Diversity and spillover risk of Swine Acute Diarrhea Syndrome (SADS) and related coronaviruses in China and Southeast Asia—analyzing 523 coronavirus sequences, including 186 new bat-derived genomes. The work maps diversity, evolution, and spillover risk to pigs and humans, identifying hotspots in southern China, northern Vietnam, Java, and central Thailand. Key collaborations acknowledged with the Wuhan Institute of Virology and Kunming Institute of Zoology, including Ben Hu, Bei Li, Wei Zhang, and Zheng-Li Shi. Funding includes Samuel Freeman Charitable Trust, The Wallace Fund, an anonymous Schwab Charitable Fund donor, NIH grants R01AI110964 and U01AI151797, and USAID PREDICT. NHG emerged in April 2025 after EcoHealth Alliance suspended operations. The study notes SADS-CoV originated in bats and caused porcine outbreaks in China, with potential human cell infection in vitro. Daszak continues coronavirus research via NHG.
notes: 本記事は新規感染症アウトブレイクの報告ではなく、SADS-CoV（豚急性下痢症候群コロナウイルス）に関する研究論文の紹介。Peter Daszak氏（元EcoHealth Alliance）がNature Health Globalを通じて武漢ウイルス研究所等と継続的にコロナウイルス研究を実施している点が報じられている。SADS-CoVのヒト細胞への感染可能性がin vitroで示唆されているが、実際のヒト感染事例は報告されていない。情報源はフランス語の非主流メディアであり、信頼性の検証が必要。

articleSummary: Syphilis among Thai teens has surged tenfold over the past decade, rising from 14.41 to 134.68 cases per 100,000 people in Thailand. The Department of Disease Control cites behavioral and environmental changes among youth, urging comprehensive sexual health education, greater condom access, and stigma-free testing. Syphilis is sexually transmitted and can spread via blood transfusion or mother-to-child transmission. Early signs include a genital ulcer; later, rashes may appear on the body, including palms and soles, with patchy hair loss in some cases. Some individuals remain asymptomatic for years, and untreated infection can damage the brain, heart, and blood vessels after about a decade. Diagnosis is typically by blood tests, such as prenatal or pre-donation screening. Cure is possible with proper treatment and ongoing follow-up serology; community involvement is essential for prevention.
notes: 10年間で10倍増（14.41→134.68/10万人）は顕著な増加傾向。タイ疾病管理局が若者の行動・環境変化を要因として指摘し、性教育・コンドームアクセス・スティグマフリーの検査を推進。急性アウトブレイクではなく慢性的な公衆衛生課題として位置づけられる。

articleHeadline: 3 Vietnamese children suspected of botulinum poisoning after eating fermented fish
articleSummary: Three boys in Da Nang City, central Vietnam, were hospitalized with suspected botulinum food poisoning after eating 'ca u chua', a fermented fish dish from Quang Nam highlands. Six family members who shared the meal on Saturday fell ill; by 6:00 pm three children, H.N.T., 15; H.Q.N., 7; H.Q.B., 11, developed abdominal pain, vomiting and fatigue. The 15-year-old was admitted in a coma with breathing difficulties, dilated pupils, weak pulse and bladder loss, placed on a ventilator; plasma exchange with albumin was performed after consultation with Cho Ray Hospital specialists in Ho Chi Minh City. The two younger boys showed ptosis, muscle weakness and breathing problems; one required mechanical ventilation, the other assisted breathing. All were transferred to Da Nang Hospital for Women and Children. The dish, made from fermenting freshwater fish with rice, salt and spices, has been linked to several botulinum cases recently, including a 2023 Phuoc Son incident.

articleSummary: On 9 March 2026, a girl born in 2020 from Kim Phú commune, Quảng Trị Province, Vietnam, died four months after a dog bite in December 2025. articleSummary: Hepatitis B concerns arise in Rahimabad’s Tarouna and Jalamau villages. Separately, Balrampur Hospital’s open-PPP dialysis unit (14 machines; 18 patients registered) raised infection concerns for Hepatitis B and C among dialyzed patients; three years ago more than 30 patients in the unit became HBV infected, suggesting possible in-dialysis transmission. Some relatives allege testing-related issues and procedural lapses.

articleHeadline: Everest Spices Under Scanner After Lab Tests Flag Pesticides: What Is Enterobacteriaceae Bacteria
articleSummary: On 11 March 2026, a YouTube video by Trustified alleged Everest spice products failed independent laboratory tests purchased from a D-Mart store in India, raising questions about FSSAI safety compliance. The spices tested were Everest Garam Masala, Kitchen King Masala, Kashmiri Lal Chilli Powder, and Meat Masala. Reported findings claimed pesticide levels above safety limits in Garam Masala (Acetamiprid, Azoxystrobin) and Meat Masala (Ethion, Tebuconazole, Azoxystrobin, Fluopyram), with samples showing elevated Enterobacteriaceae. Kitchen King Masala also exceeded Enterobacteriaceae limits, while Kashmiri Lal Chilli Powder had no pesticides above limits but elevated Enterobacteriaceae. The claims suggest contamination during processing or handling and hygiene lapses. Health implications cited include stomach infections from Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Salmonella) causing diarrhoea, vomiting, and abdominal pain; pesticide residues may affect liver, intestines, and nervous system, with higher risk for children, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The findings remain unverified by official agencies at this time.
